title: OCD 2 — Test
src: Developmental disturbances of shape, size, number & structure of teeth

mcqs.q: The most common site of localized microdontia is the:
mcqs.explain: Localized microdontia most often affects the maxillary lateral incisor (the “peg lateral”), then the maxillary third molar.

mcqs.q: True generalized microdontia is classically seen in:
mcqs.explain: True generalized microdontia (all teeth small) occurs in pituitary dwarfism; gigantism gives macrodontia.

mcqs.q: Another term used for macrodontia is:
mcqs.explain: Macrodontia (teeth larger than normal) is also called megadontia.

mcqs.q: Fusion is best defined as:
opts: Union of two tooth germs into one structure
mcqs.explain: Fusion = union of two adjacent germs during development, producing a single large tooth.

mcqs.q: On counting the teeth, fusion typically gives:
mcqs.explain: Because two germs join into one tooth, the arch has one fewer tooth than normal.

mcqs.q: This radiograph shows a double tooth with separate canals. The anomaly is:
mcqs.explain: A double tooth formed by union of two germs is fusion; counting shows one tooth fewer.

mcqs.q: Gemination differs from fusion because the tooth count is:
mcqs.explain: Gemination is an attempt of a single germ to divide, giving one extra structure → one tooth more on counting.

mcqs.q: Concrescence is the union of teeth by:
opts: Cementum, after root formation is complete
mcqs.explain: Concrescence = roots joined by cementum after root formation; extracting one may remove the other.

mcqs.q: A sharp bend of up to 90° at the crown–root junction is called:
mcqs.explain: Dilaceration is a severe bend in the long axis (up to 90°), usually from trauma during root development.

mcqs.q: This extracted tooth shows a severe root bend. It is an example of:
mcqs.explain: A marked bend at the crown–root junction is dilaceration, which complicates extraction and endodontics.

mcqs.q: Taurodontism (“bull-like teeth”) shows:
opts: A long pulp chamber with apically displaced furcation and short roots
mcqs.explain: Taurodont molars have elongated crowns, apically placed furcation, a long pulp chamber and short roots.

mcqs.q: This radiograph shows an elongated pulp chamber with a low furcation. It is:
mcqs.explain: An enlarged, apically extended pulp chamber with short roots is taurodontism, seen in Down and Klinefelter syndromes.

mcqs.q: A talon cusp is most associated with which syndrome?
mcqs.explain: The talon cusp (an extra cusp from the cingulum of an incisor) is prevalent in Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome.

mcqs.q: “Leong's premolar” (occlusal enamel projection that may contain a pulp horn) is:
mcqs.explain: Dens evaginatus is an occlusal enamel tubercle on premolars (Leong's premolar) that may contain a pulp horn.

mcqs.q: “A tooth within a tooth” (dens invaginatus) most commonly affects the:
mcqs.explain: Dens in dente is an exaggerated enamel-lined lingual pit, usually noted in the maxillary lateral incisor.

mcqs.q: This diagram shows an enamel-lined invagination into the crown. It is:
mcqs.explain: An invagination of the crown surface lined by enamel (“tooth within a tooth”) is dens invaginatus.

mcqs.q: Enamel pearls (enamelomas) are nodules of enamel found:
opts: On the root, near the CEJ
mcqs.explain: Enamel pearls are small enamel nodules on the root close to or at the cemento-enamel junction.

mcqs.q: Complete anodontia is classically associated with:
mcqs.explain: Rare complete anodontia is associated with hereditary ectodermal dysplasia; partial anodontia = hypodontia.

mcqs.q: Partial anodontia is also called:
mcqs.explain: Hypodontia = partial anodontia (a few teeth missing). False = post-extraction; pseudo = unerupted.

mcqs.q: Anodontia results from failure of which stage of odontogenesis?
mcqs.explain: Congenitally missing teeth arise from a defect in the initiation stage of tooth development.

mcqs.q: The most common supernumerary tooth is the:
mcqs.explain: The mesiodens (between the maxillary central incisors) is the commonest supernumerary tooth, followed by para/distomolars.

mcqs.q: The most accepted cause of supernumerary teeth is:
mcqs.explain: Supernumerary (extra) teeth are attributed to hyperactivity of the dental lamina.

mcqs.q: This image shows extra teeth in the maxilla. They are:
mcqs.explain: Additional teeth beyond the normal complement are supernumerary teeth (e.g. mesiodens).

mcqs.q: Multiple supernumerary teeth with hypoplastic/absent clavicles suggest:
mcqs.explain: Cleidocranial dysplasia: multiple supernumeraries, delayed eruption and hypoplastic/absent clavicles.

mcqs.q: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a structural defect of:
mcqs.explain: Amelogenesis imperfecta affects enamel (abnormal amelogenins) in both dentitions.

mcqs.q: In the HYPOPLASTIC type of amelogenesis imperfecta the enamel is:
mcqs.explain: Hypoplastic AI = inadequate matrix formation → thin, pitted or grooved enamel with normal dentin/pulp.

mcqs.q: This image shows yellow-brown, sensitive teeth with thin enamel. The diagnosis is:
mcqs.explain: Defective enamel that is discoloured, sensitive and caries-prone, with abnormal radiographic enamel bulk, is amelogenesis imperfecta.

mcqs.q: Dentinogenesis imperfecta is inherited as:
mcqs.explain: Dentinogenesis imperfecta (hereditary opalescent dentin) is an autosomal dominant disorder of dentin.

mcqs.q: Shields type I dentinogenesis imperfecta occurs together with:
mcqs.explain: Shields type I DI is seen with osteogenesis imperfecta; type II occurs without OI; type III = shell teeth.

mcqs.q: This panoramic image shows faint, poorly mineralised “ghost teeth”. The diagnosis is:
mcqs.explain: Regional odontodysplasia is a localized, non-hereditary defect of enamel, dentin and pulp giving a radiographic “ghost teeth” appearance.

saqs.q: Differentiate fusion, gemination and concrescence (mechanism and tooth count).
saqs.a: Fusion = union of two germs → one large tooth, one fewer on counting. Gemination = one germ splits → two crowns/one root, one more on counting. Concrescence = roots joined by cementum after root formation, count normal.

saqs.q: Define taurodontism and give two syndromes it is associated with.
saqs.a: Taurodontism = “bull-like” molars with elongated crown, apically displaced furcation, long pulp chamber and short roots. Associations: Down and Klinefelter syndromes.

saqs.q: List the three types of amelogenesis imperfecta.
saqs.a: Hypoplastic (too little matrix — thin/pitted), hypomineralized (normal amount, poorly calcified) and hypomaturative (normal at eruption, then breaks down).

saqs.q: Give the Shields classification of dentinogenesis imperfecta.
saqs.a: Type I — DI WITH osteogenesis imperfecta; Type II — DI WITHOUT OI; Type III — “shell teeth” (brandywine).

saqs.q: What are the two types of dentin dysplasia?
saqs.a: Type I = “rootless teeth” (very short roots, mobile teeth). Type II = “thistle-tube” shaped pulp chamber.

saqs.q: What is regional odontodysplasia and its hallmark radiographic feature?
saqs.a: A localized, non-hereditary defect affecting enamel, dentin and pulp; radiographs show “ghost teeth” (wide pulp, open apices, poor enamel–dentin contrast).
